name: Lagoon blue
lede: Lagoon blue is a saturated teal-blue named for the shallow, light-filled water of a lagoon, a vivid greenish blue by the ISCC-NBS classification.

sections.title: A landscape word
sections.body:
ColorHub's library carries Lagoon blue as a landscape name, grouped with words for a place or a body of water rather than a pigment or a person [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[sky-steel]], [[bluish-steel-blue]], [[capri-blue]] and [[sea-teal]], at 5.5, 5.5, 6.4 and 6.5 ΔE [1]. The ISCC-NBS system would file the hex #0093AF as a vivid greenish blue, a measured distance of 7.4 units from its nearest official block [2]. In Munsell terms it lands near 4.9B 5.5/7.4, a mid-value, strongly saturated blue-green [2]. Who first wrote the two words together as a color name is not recorded in our sources, so the coinage stays undocumented here [1].

The word itself tracks a real body of water: a lagoon is shallow enough that sunlight reaches the pale sand below, which is what gives real lagoons their saturated turquoise-to-blue range rather than the deep navy of open ocean. Look for that same light-struck quality in [[turquoise]] and [[persian-green]], its closer relatives on the color wheel.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Lagoon blue in 11 of 23,781 paintings, 0.05 percent, with the stricter within-painting test narrowing that to 4 [3]. That makes it rarer than about 77 percent of the named colors we track [3]. The earliest match, as photographed, is a 1528 painting attributed to Andrea del Sarto, though the archive's early centuries are thin enough that this is a floor, not a true first [3]. Inside the paintings that do carry it, the color most often sits as a mid-tone or a light passage rather than a shadow, about 75 percent of the time combined [3]. In printed English the phrase "lagoon blue" peaked in the 1960s, a rise Google's book scans tie to the all-senses use of the word, since lagoon is also a place name that can skew the count [4]. All matches are computed against photographs of varnished, aged canvases, not pigment identifications [3].
